headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network tools make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cline can read/write workspace files and use MCP, while OpenHands can read/write files in its runtime and also use MCP. The pair has a filesystem bridge and both can ingest file content, so malicious instructions in shared artifacts could be parsed as trusted content. This is not proven to be automatic cross-ingestion, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or mounted volume, injected instructions in files can cross from one agent to the other.
IF either agent is configured to treat file contents as authoritative prompts, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces so the agents never read each other's files.
Disable MCP servers unless explicitly needed.
Add a manual review step for any file that contains instructions or HTML.
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for agent-generated files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cline shares state via filesystem and touches source code and browser screenshots; OpenHands shares state via mounted volume and touches files in the runtime sandbox. If sensitive files are present in the shared workspace, either agent can expose them through its outputs or model-provider calls. The leakage path exists in default-style workspace sharing, but the blast radius is bounded to the mounted data.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared workspace or mounted volume, both agents can access them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to its model provider, those contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces.
Use separate mounts for each agent.
Redact sensitive files before opening the workspace.
Restrict model-provider access to non-sensitive projects.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, and modify_git_state, and both can operate on shared state via filesystem or mounted volume. Concurrent edits to the same repo or workspace can overwrite each other or corrupt git state without a locking primitive being stated in either profile. This is a direct overlap with high-risk mutable resources.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or directory, concurrent writes can conflict.
IF both agents commit or rebase without external locking, repository state can be corrupted.
mitigations: Run the agents on separate branches.
Assign disjoint directories.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use a lock file around git operations.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cline and OpenHands both act as autonomous coding agents with shell, browser, and MCP tools, so one agent's output can easily become the other's input. Neither profile shows a built-in verification gate that would prevent B from trusting A's generated code, commands, or facts. That makes cascading mistakes plausible in default workflows, though not necessarily irreversible.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes Cline-generated code or commands without independent verification, errors can propagate.
IF Cline uses OpenHands-produced artifacts as authoritative, downstream actions may repeat mistakes.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Compare outputs against a second source.
Limit one agent to drafting only.
Disable auto-apply of patches.
requires-engineering: add validation checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source coding agents with similar broad tool access and no stated residency, certification, or retention mismatch. The profiles do not show a compliance conflict by themselves, so only a low residual risk remains from unspecified deployment choices. The other agent is cited because the assessment is pairwise, but no mismatch is evidenced.
conditions: IF one deployment stores regulated data while the other has a stricter retention or residency policy, compliance risk increases.
IF either agent is configured with a third-party model provider under a different policy, policy mismatch may arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Align retention settings before use.
Document the model-provider policy for both agents.
Review where logs are stored.
requires-engineering: implement policy-aware routing and retention controls.
